newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court denies state's school prayer appeal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court denies state's school prayer appeal.

text.p: The Supreme Court rejected Monday an appeal by Mississippi seeking to reinstate a state law allowing student-led prayer in public schools.
The justices let stand a U.S. appeals court ruling that struck down the 1994 law for violating the constitutional requirement on the separation between church and state.

The law required public schools to allow invocations, benedictions and "nonsectarian, nonproselytizing, student-initiated prayer" at all school-related student events. It covered compulsory and non-compulsory events in and outside schools including student assemblies and sporting events.

The law had been adopted after a high school principal in Jackson allowed students to recite prayers over the public address system during the school day. He was disciplined for the widely publicised incident.
The Supreme Court in a landmark 1962 decision outlawed teacher-led prayer in public schools but conservative religious groups have been trying to put prayers back in schools.

A challenge to the Mississippi law was filed before the start of the 1994-95 school year on behalf of students enrolled in the Jackson public schools, their parents and the American Civil Liberties Union.

A federal judge immediately halted enforcement of the law except for voluntary, student-led prayers at high school commencements. The appeals court in January upheld the decision, ruling that the law represented an unconstitutional government effort to advance religion.

Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore defended the law, saying nothing in the measure "directs, coerces or compels" students to initiate any prayer. "The statute on its face does not mandate that any religious speech or prayer occur at all at any time -- instead this is left to private choice," he said in asking the Supreme Court to hear the case.

"In a public school climate characterised by a recent dramatic increase in teenagers' drug use, and in which a loss of moral values, lack of respect for authority and violence are all too prevalent, a court-sponsored message of hostility to student-initiated prayer and religious viewpoints is exactly the wrong message," he said.

Attorneys for those challenging the law urged the Supreme Court to deny the appeal, arguing that Mississippi "failed to advance a sound reason" for further review of the case. They said the appeals court decision was consistent with Supreme Court precedent and emphasised the ruling does not affect the existing rights of students to engage in the free exercise of religion and free speech.
The Supreme Court turned down Mississippi's appeal without any comment or dissent.
